beats.text: November, 1952. A C.I.A. radio picks up a message from deep inside China.
That summer, the C.I.A. had dropped a spy team into Manchuria. Now, one man had to come out.
There was no runway. Just two poles in the snow, a rope between them, and a man strapped to it.
A plane swoops in low, hooks the rope, and yanks him into the sky.
In the back, two young C.I.A. officers, John Downey and Richard Fecteau, wait to reel him in.
Midnight. A bright moon. The plane slows almost to a stall.
Then, white sheets fly off the snow. Under them, two anti-aircraft guns.
The team had already been captured. The call for help was bait.
Both pilots died. Downey and Fecteau were taken alive.
America said they were army civilians, lost at sea. For twenty years, it never said C.I.A.
Asked for the names of his C.I.A. classmates, Fecteau gave them his college football team.
Fecteau walked free in 1971. Downey, in 1973, after Nixon finally admitted the truth.
Downey became a judge. And he married a woman born in Manchuria, near the field where his plane went down.
